parsed_answer.content: In high-concurrency Java applications, AtomicLong relies on a single volatile variable and a compare-and-swap (CAS) loop to manage state. While efficient under low contention, it suffers from severe performance degradation when multiple threads attempt to update the same memory location simultaneously. Each thread competes for the same cache line, causing 'cache line bouncing' or 'false sharing' at the CPU level, where the L1/L2 caches must constantly invalidate and synchronize across cores, effectively serializing execution. LongAdder, introduced in Java 8, solves this by applying the principle of striping. Instead of a single counter, it maintains a lazily initialized array of cells (Striped64). Each thread maps to a specific cell based on its thread ID, reducing contention by distributing updates across multiple memory locations. When the JVM detects contention, it dynamically grows the cell array to further spread the load, only collapsing these values into a single sum when the user explicitly calls sum().

items: LongAdder uses the @Contended annotation on its internal Cell class to prevent false sharing by padding the memory layout, ensuring that different cells do not reside on the same CPU cache line.
The 'sum()' operation is not atomic across the entire array; it is a point-in-time snapshot. If updates occur during the summation, the result may not include those concurrent increments.
LongAdder dynamically resizes the cell array based on the number of available processors, capped at the nearest power of two, which minimizes the probability of hash collisions between threads.
Under extremely low contention, LongAdder falls back to updating a 'base' variable, mimicking AtomicLong behavior to avoid the overhead of cell array management.

parsed_answer.content: Do not swap AtomicLong for LongAdder blindly. If your application requires strict, linearizable updates (e.g., a sequence generator or a value that must be checked immediately after increment), AtomicLong is mandatory. LongAdder is strictly for 'summation' use cases like request counters or statistics where eventual consistency of the total is acceptable.

title: How does LongAdder scale better than AtomicLong under high contention?
